claim: Lentiviral vectors can be adapted as carriers of designer nuclease proteins, providing efficient targeted gene disruption in vector-treated cell lines and primary cells.
source: In this study, we adapt lentiviral vectors as carriers of designer nuclease proteins, providing efficient targeted gene disruption in vector-treated cell lines and primary cells.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Co-packaging pairs of ZFN proteins with donor RNA in 'all-in-one' lentiviral particles enables co-delivery of ZFN proteins and the donor template for homology-directed repair leading to targeted DNA insertion and gene correction.
source: By co-packaging pairs of ZFN proteins with donor RNA in 'all-in-one' lentiviral particles, we co-deliver ZFN proteins and the donor template for homology-directed repair leading to targeted DNA insertion and gene correction.
evidence: The abstract describes this as a key finding, with supporting experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ZFN protein transduction demonstrates reduced off-target activity relative to conventional delivery approaches in comparative studies of ZFN activity at a predetermined target locus and a known nearby off-target locus.
source: Comparative studies of ZFN activity in a predetermined target locus and a known nearby off-target locus demonstrate reduced off-target activity after ZFN protein transduction relative to conventional delivery approaches.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 comparing LP-delivered and plasmid-encoded ZFNs.

claim: TALEN proteins can be delivered by protein transduction using lentiviral particles.
source: Additionally, TALEN proteins are added to the repertoire of custom-designed nucleases that can be delivered by protein transduction.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, with supporting experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ZFNs and TALENs are chimeric nucleases composed of a custom-designed DNA binding domain fused to the DNA-cleavage domain from the FokI endonuclease that upon dimer formation cleaves the DNA.
source: ZFNs and TALENs are chimeric nucleases composed of a custom-designed DNA binding domain fused to the DNA-cleavage domain from the FokI endonuclease that upon dimer formation cleaves the DNA.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the structure and function of ZFNs and TALENs.

claim: ZFN- and TALEN-induced DSBs trigger genome editing through cellular repair mechanisms involving either error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR) with an available DNA donor template.
source: ZFN- and TALEN-induced DSBs trigger genome editing through cellular repair mechanisms involving either error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR) with an available DNA donor template.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms following nuclease-induced double-strand breaks.

claim: Designer nucleases have broad applications in biological experimentation.
source: Designer nucleases have broad applications in biological experimentation (Urnov et al., 2010; Bogdanove and Voytas, 2011) and have been successfully utilized for the production of gene knockout model animals (Doyon et al., 2008; Geurts et al., 2009; Tesson et al., 2011) and in emerging gene therapies (Perez et al., 2008; Li et al., 2011, 2013; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Designer nucleases have been successfully utilized for the production of gene knockout model animals.
source: Designer nucleases have broad applications in biological experimentation (Urnov et al., 2010; Bogdanove and Voytas, 2011) and have been successfully utilized for the production of gene knockout model animals (Doyon et al., 2008; Geurts et al., 2009; Tesson et al., 2011) and in emerging gene therapies (Perez et al., 2008; Li et al., 2011, 2013; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Doyon et al., 2008; Geurts et al., 2009; Tesson et al., 2011).

claim: Designer nucleases have been used in emerging gene therapies.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Perez et al., 2008; Li et al., 2011, 2013; Sun et al., 2012).

claim: ZFNs and TALENs have been administered to cells by transfection or electroporation of nucleic acids, DNA or RNA, encoding a pair of nuclease proteins.
source: Thus far, ZFNs and TALENs have been administered to cells by transfection or electroporation of nucleic acids, DNA or RNA, encoding a pair of nuclease proteins (Urnov et al., 2005; Miller et al., 2011; Carlson et al., 2012) or by exploiting viral gene vehicles such as integrase-deficient lentiviral vectors (IDLVs) (Lombardo et al., 2007), adeno-associated virus-derived vectors (AAV vectors) (Ellis et al., 2013), or adenoviral vectors (Holkers et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Urnov et al., 2005; Miller et al., 2011; Carlson et al., 2012).

claim: ZFNs and TALENs have been administered to cells by exploiting viral gene vehicles such as integrase-deficient lentiviral vectors (IDLVs).
source: Thus far, ZFNs and TALENs have been administered to cells by transfection or electroporation of nucleic acids, DNA or RNA, encoding a pair of nuclease proteins (Urnov et al., 2005; Miller et al., 2011; Carlson et al., 2012) or by exploiting viral gene vehicles such as integrase-deficient lentiviral vectors (IDLVs) (Lombardo et al., 2007), adeno-associated virus-derived vectors (AAV vectors) (Ellis et al., 2013), or adenoviral vectors (Holkers et al., 2013).

claim: Successful administration of ZFN- or TALEN-encoding genes leads to high intracellular levels of nucleases.
source: Successful administration of ZFN- or TALEN-encoding genes leads to high intracellular levels of nucleases and furthermore imposes a risk of random insertion in the genome, resulting potentially in prolonged nuclease expression and accumulating events of off-target cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of gene delivery methods and their known consequences.

claim: Administration of ZFN- or TALEN-encoding genes imposes a risk of random insertion in the genome, resulting potentially in prolonged nuclease expression and accumulating events of off-target cleavage.
source: Successful administration of ZFN- or TALEN-encoding genes leads to high intracellular levels of nucleases and furthermore imposes a risk of random insertion in the genome, resulting potentially in prolonged nuclease expression and accumulating events of off-target cleavage.

claim: ZFNs have been fused to destabilizing domains regulated by small molecules to attenuate ZFN toxicity.
source: Towards this goal, ZFNs have been fused to destabilizing domains regulated by small molecules to attenuate ZFN toxicity (Pruett-Miller et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Pruett-Miller et al., 2009).

claim: Targeted gene disruption has been achieved by direct cellular delivery of purified ZFN proteins by exploiting the cell-penetrating capability of ZFNs.
source: Moreover, by exploiting the cell-penetrating capability of ZFNs, targeted gene disruption has recently been achieved by direct cellular delivery of purified ZFN proteins (Gaj et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Gaj et al., 2012).

claim: Direct cellular delivery of purified ZFN proteins may require multiple treatments due to the reduced cellular uptake of proteins.
source: Although such approach may require multiple treatments due to the reduced cellular uptake of proteins (Mellert et al., 2012), recent findings suggest that ZFN uptake may be further improved by ligand-mediated endocytosis (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Mellert et al., 2012).

claim: ZFN uptake may be improved by ligand-mediated endocytosis.
source: Although such approach may require multiple treatments due to the reduced cellular uptake of proteins (Mellert et al., 2012), recent findings suggest that ZFN uptake may be further improved by ligand-mediated endocytosis (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Chen et al., 2013).

claim: Retroviruses can tolerate the incorporation of heterologous proteins.
source: It has been known for decades that retroviruses can tolerate the incorporation of heterologous proteins (Jones et al., 1990; Weldon et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Jones et al., 1990; Weldon et al., 1990).

claim: Lentiviral particles (LPs) have been engineered to carry foreign proteins for the purpose of visualizing the intracellular behavior of the virus during infection.
source: Lentiviral particles (LPs) have been engineered to carry foreign proteins for the purpose of visualizing the intracellular behavior of the virus during infection (McDonald et al., 2002; Jouvenet et al., 2008) and altering the viral integration profile (Bushman, 1994; Goulaouic and Chow, 1996; Bushman and Miller, 1997), as well as for ferrying antiviral (Okui et al., 2000; Ao et al., 2008) and antitumor (Link et al., 2006; Miyauchi et al., 2012) protein therapeutics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (McDonald et al., 2002; Jouvenet et al., 2008).

claim: Lentiviral particles have been engineered to carry foreign proteins for altering the viral integration profile.
source: Lentiviral particles (LPs) have been engineered to carry foreign proteins for the purpose of visualizing the intracellular behavior of the virus during infection (McDonald et al., 2002; Jouvenet et al., 2008) and altering the viral integration profile (Bushman, 1994; Goulaouic and Chow, 1996; Bushman and Miller, 1997), as well as for ferrying antiviral (Okui et al., 2000; Ao et al., 2008) and antitumor (Link et al., 2006; Miyauchi et al., 2012) protein therapeutics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Bushman, 1994; Goulaouic and Chow, 1996; Bushman and Miller, 1997).

source: Lentiviral particles (LPs) have been engineered to carry foreign proteins for the purpose of visualizing the intracellular behavior of the virus during infection (McDonald et al., 2002; Jouvenet et al., 2008) and altering the viral integration profile (Bushman, 1994; Goulaouic and Chow, 1996; Bushman and Miller, 1997), as well as for ferrying antiviral (Okui et al., 2000; Ao et al., 2008) and antitumor (Link et al., 2006; Miyauchi et al., 2012) protein therapeutics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Okui et al., 2000; Ao et al., 2008).

claim: Lentiviral particles have been engineered to carry foreign proteins for ferrying antitumor protein therapeutics.
source: Lentiviral particles (LPs) have been engineered to carry foreign proteins for the purpose of visualizing the intracellular behavior of the virus during infection (McDonald et al., 2002; Jouvenet et al., 2008) and altering the viral integration profile (Bushman, 1994; Goulaouic and Chow, 1996; Bushman and Miller, 1997), as well as for ferrying antiviral (Okui et al., 2000; Ao et al., 2008) and antitumor (Link et al., 2006; Miyauchi et al., 2012) protein therapeutics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Link et al., 2006; Miyauchi et al., 2012).

claim: The accessory HIV-1 protein Vpr was adapted as a carrier of fused proteins in early strategies for transducing heterologous protein cargo.
source: In early strategies, the accessory HIV-1 protein Vpr was adapted as a carrier of fused proteins (Wu et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Wu et al., 1995).

claim: Vpr fusions have been shown to ferry Cre recombinase into transduced cells.
source: Recently, Vpr fusions have been shown also to ferry Cre recombinase (Michel et al., 2010) and I-SceI meganuclease (Izmiryan et al., 2011) into transduced cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Michel et al., 2010).

claim: Vpr fusions have been shown to ferry I-SceI meganuclease into transduced cells.
source: Recently, Vpr fusions have been shown also to ferry Cre recombinase (Michel et al., 2010) and I-SceI meganuclease (Izmiryan et al., 2011) into transduced cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Izmiryan et al., 2011).

claim: HIV-1 virions incorporate approximately 700 copies of Vpr per virion.
source: However, HIV-1 virions incorporate relatively few copies of Vpr (estimated 700 copies Vpr per virion [Swanson and Malim, 2008]), and the therapeutic potential of such approach may be hampered further by the known toxicity of the Vpr protein (Tachiwana et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Swanson and Malim, 2008).

claim: The therapeutic potential of Vpr-based protein delivery may be hampered by the known toxicity of the Vpr protein.
source: However, HIV-1 virions incorporate relatively few copies of Vpr (estimated 700 copies Vpr per virion [Swanson and Malim, 2008]), and the therapeutic potential of such approach may be hampered further by the known toxicity of the Vpr protein (Tachiwana et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Tachiwana et al., 2006).

claim: Nonviral proteins may be packaged in LPs as part of the Gag polypeptide, as was previously shown for reporter proteins like GFP.
source: Alternatively, nonviral proteins may be packaged in LPs as part of the Gag polypeptide, as was previously shown for reporter proteins like GFP (Aoki et al., 2011) and the apoptosis-inducing caspase 3 protein (Miyauchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Aoki et al., 2011).

claim: Nonviral proteins may be packaged in LPs as part of the Gag polypeptide, as was previously shown for the apoptosis-inducing caspase 3 protein.
source: Alternatively, nonviral proteins may be packaged in LPs as part of the Gag polypeptide, as was previously shown for reporter proteins like GFP (Aoki et al., 2011) and the apoptosis-inducing caspase 3 protein (Miyauchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Miyauchi et al., 2012).

claim: Each HIV-1 virion contains approximately 5000 copies of Gag and 250 copies of GagPol.
source: It is estimated that each virion contains 5000 copies of Gag and 250 copies of GagPol (Swanson and Malim, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Swanson and Malim, 2008).

claim: LPs have been adapted for the delivery of the piggybac DNA transposase, which was released from Gag in a protease-dependent manner and found to facilitate efficient DNA transposition in transduced cells.
source: We recently adapted LPs for the delivery of the piggybac DNA transposase (Cai et al., 2014). The transposase was released from Gag in the virus particles in a protease-dependent manner and found to be able to facilitate efficient DNA transposition in transduced cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Cai et al., 2014).

claim: Heterologous proteins fused to the integrase in the Pol region of the GagPol polypeptide were successfully delivered by protein transduction.
source: In yet another strategy, heterologous proteins fused to the integrase in the Pol region of the GagPol polypeptide were successfully delivered by protein transduction (Schenkwein et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Schenkwein et al., 2010).

claim: ZFN proteins fused to lentiviral Gag precursors are released from the Gag and GagPol polypeptides during particle maturation.
source: For both ZFN-loaded LPs, we detected HA-tagged ZFNs of the predicted, full-length size (∼37.5 kDa), demonstrating that the majority of the virion-associated ZFNs was correctly released from the Gag and GagPol polypeptides during particle maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Release of ZFN and p24 from ZFN-PH-GagPol polypeptides is dependent on the HIV-1 protease.
source: Release of ZFN and p24 (Figure 1B,C, left and right panels, respectively) from ZFN-PH-GagPol polypeptides was inhibited by treatment of the virus-producing cells with the HIV-1 protease inhibitor Saquinavir (SQV), confirming that polypeptide cleavage, and the resulting release of ZFN proteins, was dependent on the HIV-1 protease.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B,C demonstrating inhibition by Saquinavir.

claim: ZFN protein transduction causes dose-dependent cleavage of egfp as measured by detection of NHEJ-induced sequence alterations using the Surveyor nuclease assay.
source: ZFN protein transduction caused dose-dependent cleavage of egfp as measured by detection of NHEJ-induced sequence alterations using the Surveyor nuclease assay (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Among 42 analyzed clones from cells treated with 600 ng p24 LP-ZFNLR(gfp), 8 were found to contain egfp gene disruptions, providing an unbiased disruption frequency of 19%.
source: Among a total of 42 analyzed clones, 8 were found to contain egfp gene disruptions, providing an unbiased disruption frequency of 19% (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in Table 1 and Table 1—source data 1.

claim: ZFN-directed cleavage and subsequent error-prone repair by NHEJ is detectable as early as 12 hr posttransduction.
source: Notably, ZFN-directed cleavage and subsequent error-prone repair by NHEJ was detectable as early as 12 hr posttransduction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LP-delivered pairs of ZFNs targeting CCR5 and AAVS1 loci cause significant levels of disruption in HEK293 cells, normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDFs), and primary human keratinocytes (HKs) in an LP dose-dependent manner.
source: For both loci and in all cell types, we observed significant levels of disruption and found that such disruption occurred in an LP dose-dependent manner (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The percentage of sequenced clones harboring targeted disruptions in the CCR5 locus ranges from 17% in HEK293 cells and NHDFs to 24% in primary HKs.
source: For the three cell types, the percentage of sequenced clones harboring targeted disruptions in the CCR5 locus ranged from 17% in HEK293 cells and NHDFs to 24% in primary HKs, whereas from 13% to 20% of the analyzed AAVS1 loci, depending on the cell type, harbored indels.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in Table 1 and Table 1—source data 2.

claim: From 13% to 20% of the analyzed AAVS1 loci, depending on the cell type, harbor indels after treatment with LP-ZFNLR(AAVS1).
source: For the three cell types, the percentage of sequenced clones harboring targeted disruptions in the CCR5 locus ranged from 17% in HEK293 cells and NHDFs to 24% in primary HKs, whereas from 13% to 20% of the analyzed AAVS1 loci, depending on the cell type, harbored indels.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in Table 1 and Table 1—source data 3.

claim: At a dose of 300 ng p24, LP-ZFNLR(gfp) induces a level of repair that is comparable to that obtained by the efficient co-transfection of plasmid DNA encoding the two ZFNs.
source: Hence, at a dose of 300 ng p24, LP-ZFNLR(gfp) induced a level of repair that was comparable to that obtained by the efficient co-transfection of plasmid DNA encoding the two ZFNs (Figure 3B, compare two right columns).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Co-delivery of IDLV/donor and LP-ZFNLR(gfp) to HEK293-eGFPmut cells induces gene repair, whereas neither IDLV/donor nor LP-ZFNLR(gfp) alone induces significant levels of eGFP expression.
source: Co-delivery of IDLV/donor and LP-ZFNLR(gfp) to the HEK293-eGFPmut cells induced gene repair, whereas neither IDLV/donor nor LP-ZFNLR(gfp) alone induced significant levels of eGFP expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Co-transduction with two IDLVs (IDLV-ZFNL(gfp)/donor and IDLV-ZFNR(gfp)/donor) induces eGFP expression in about 4% of treated cells, whereas neither of the two vectors alone causes gene editing.
source: Induced eGFP expression was observed only in cells treated with both IDLVs, indicative of active editing in about 4% of the treated cells, whereas neither of the two vectors alone caused gene editing (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment of HEK293-eGFPmut cells with 'all-in-one' IDLVs (IDLV-ZFNLR(gfp)/donor) results in potent induction of eGFP expression in a vector dose-dependent manner, leading to editing in more than 8% of the cells treated with ZFN-loaded IDLVs corresponding to 600 ng p24.
source: Treatment of the HEK293-eGFPmut cells with this vector resulted in potent induction of eGFP expression in a vector dose-dependent manner, leading to editing at most in more than 8% of the cells treated with ZFN-loaded IDLVs corresponding to 600 ng p24 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The overall transduction capacity of ZFN-loaded IDLVs is reduced more than fivefold relative to standard IDLVs.
source: Using this approach, we determined MOIs of 9.2 and 1.7 for IDLV/donor and IDLV-ZFNLR(gfp)/donor, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that the overall transduction capacity of ZFN-loaded IDLVs was reduced more than fivefold relative to standard IDLVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: IDLV/donor samples contain 3.1 × 10^4 infectious units (IU)/ng p24.
source: It is directly deduced from these analyses that IDLV/donor samples contain 3.1 × 104 infectious units (IU)/ng p24, whereas preparations of IDLV-ZFNLR(gfp)/donor contain an estimated 5.7 × 103 IU/ng p24 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data and calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Preparations of IDLV-ZFNLR(gfp)/donor contain an estimated 5.7 × 10^3 IU/ng p24.
source: It is directly deduced from these analyses that IDLV/donor samples contain 3.1 × 104 infectious units (IU)/ng p24, whereas preparations of IDLV-ZFNLR(gfp)/donor contain an estimated 5.7 × 103 IU/ng p24 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data and calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Editing of the egfp gene is absent when the particles are not pseudotyped with VSV-G and therefore incapable of transducing the cells.
source: Importantly, editing of the egfp gene was absent when the particles were not pseudotyped with VSV-G and therefore incapable of transducing the cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Pretreatment of reporter cells with Bafilomycin A1 (Baf A1), an inhibitor of endosomal escape, markedly reduces the level of editing.
source: Furthermore, pretreatment of the reporter cells with Bafilomycin A1 (Baf A1), an inhibitor of endosomal escape, markedly reduced the level of editing (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 'All-in-one' lentiviral vectors containing both ZFN proteins and the donor sequence facilitate high levels of targeted gene repair in a manner that depends on the dose and VSV-G-mediated endocytosis.
source: We conclude that 'all-in-one' lentiviral vectors containing both ZFN proteins and the donor sequence facilitate high levels of targeted gene repair in a manner that depends on the dose and VSV-G-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Site-directed editing facilitated by HR of both the CCR5 and AAVS1 loci is observed in HEK293 cells and NHDFs after treatment with 'all-in-one' IDLVs at an MOI of 34.
source: By PCR amplification using primers recognizing the LS and sequences outside the homology arm, we observed site-directed editing facilitated by HR of both the CCR5 and AAVS1 loci in HEK293 cells and NHDFs (Figure 3F, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Signs of editing are not evident in cells treated with preparations of IDLVs harboring only one of the ZFNs (ZFNL(CCR5) or ZFNL(AAVS1)), indicating that homology-directed insertion of the linker is achieved only after delivery of both left and right ZFN proteins.
source: Notably, signs of editing were not evident in cells treated with preparations of IDLVs harboring only one of the ZFNs (ZFNL(CCR5) or ZFNL(AAVS1)), indicating that homology-directed insertion of the linker was achieved only after delivery of both left and right ZFN proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3F and represents an inference from the negative control results.

claim: LP-TALENLR(gfp) carrying both the left and right TALEN proteins designed to recognize sequences flanking the mutations in the egfp gene induces gene disruption in HEK293-eGFPmut reporter cells.
source: Gene disruption was identified by Surveyor nuclease-directed detection of mismatches in re-annealed PCR products (Figure 4B) and confirmed by sequencing of cloned PCR products.
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 4B and sequence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 3 out of 46 sequenced alleles (6.5%) were found to contain indels as a result of treatment with LP-delivered TALEN proteins.
source: Hence, 3 out of 46 sequenced alleles (6.5%) were found to contain indels as a result of the treatment with LP-delivered TALEN proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transfecting cells with plasmid DNA containing the donor sequence prior to treatment with LP-TALENLR(gfp) results in 0.2% of the cells being eGFP positive as measured 15 days after transduction.
source: Moreover, by transfecting the cells with plasmid DNA containing the donor sequence prior to treatment of the cells with LP-TALENLR(gfp), we found that 0.2% of the cells were eGFP positive (as measured 15 days after transduction), whereas control treatments without LPs and donor DNA, respectively did not trigger eGFP expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Western blot analysis of viral particles harboring an HA-tagged version of one of the two TALEN proteins fused to the GagPol polypeptide reveals a cleavage pattern indicative of substantial proteolytic cleavage within the TALEN domain of the fusion protein, leading to truncated versions of the protein.
source: Notably, Western blot analysis of viral particles harboring an HA-tagged version of one of the two TALEN proteins fused to the GagPol polypeptide unveiled a cleavage pattern indicative of substantial proteolytic cleavage within the TALEN domain of the fusion protein, leading to truncated versions of the protein (indicated by TALEN* in Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A low level of full-length TALEN protein is evident in the particles.
source: Although a low level of full-length TALEN protein with the same mobility as HA-tagged TALEN protein expressed in cells (Figure 4E, upper band marked by 'TALEN') was indeed evident in the particles, these data indicated the presence of cryptic HIV-1 protease cleavage sites internally in the TALEN protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The presence of cryptic HIV-1 protease cleavage sites internally in the TALEN protein is indicated by Western blot analysis.
source: Although a low level of full-length TALEN protein with the same mobility as HA-tagged TALEN protein expressed in cells (Figure 4E, upper band marked by 'TALEN') was indeed evident in the particles, these data indicated the presence of cryptic HIV-1 protease cleavage sites internally in the TALEN protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TALEN-directed gene disruption and repair may be further optimized by localizing and eliminating internal protease cleavage sites.
source: This suggests that TALEN-directed gene disruption and repair may be further optimized by localizing and eliminating internal protease cleavage sites.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of internal cleavage sites.

claim: The CCR2 locus has high homology to CCR5 and has been identified as a major off-target site of CCR5-targeting ZFNs.
source: The CCR2 locus has high homology to CCR5 and has been identified as a major off-target site of CCR5-targeting ZFNs (Perez et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Perez et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2010).

claim: For the CCR5-targeting ZFNs employed in this study, only a single nucleotide differs between the CCR5 and CCR2 recognition sites of each ZFN.
source: For the CCR5-targeting ZFNs employed in this study, only a single nucleotide differs between the CCR5 and CCR2 recognition sites of each ZFN.
evidence: This is a statement about the specific ZFNs used in the study, based on sequence analysis.

claim: Off-target cleavage at the CCR2 locus is observed by both protein transduction and plasmid transfection but not in non-treated cells.
source: Indeed, we observed off-target cleavage at the CCR2 locus by both protein transduction and plasmid transfection but not in the non-treated cells (Figure 5B), indicating that both LP-delivered and DNA-encoded ZFNs induced simultaneous double-stranded DNA breaks within the CCR2 and CCR5 loci.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both LP-delivered and DNA-encoded ZFNs induce simultaneous double-stranded DNA breaks within the CCR2 and CCR5 loci.
source: Indeed, we observed off-target cleavage at the CCR2 locus by both protein transduction and plasmid transfection but not in the non-treated cells (Figure 5B), indicating that both LP-delivered and DNA-encoded ZFNs induced simultaneous double-stranded DNA breaks within the CCR2 and CCR5 loci.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Protein transduction by lentiviral particles induces significantly higher rates of on-target gene disruption than plasmid transfection under the given conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 5C (left panel) by Surveyor nuclease-directed detection of mismatches in re-annealed PCR products, protein transduction by lentiviral particles induced under the given conditions significantly higher rates of on-target gene disruption than plasmid transfection.
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: An increasing dose of ZFN-loaded LPs triggers increased off-target activity at the CCR2 locus.
source: Similarly, when we analyzed for mismatches at the CCR2 locus, an increasing dose of ZFN-loaded LPs was seen to trigger increased off-target activity (Figure 5C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A similar level of off-target activity is observed for all doses of transfected plasmid DNA, indicating that LP-delivered ZFNs even at levels that induced markedly higher levels of on-target disruption do not induce increased levels of off-target activity at the CCR2 locus.
source: Importantly, however, a similar level of off-target activity was observed for all doses of transfected plasmid DNA, indicating that LP-delivered ZFNs even at levels that induced markedly higher levels of on-target disruption did not induce increased levels of off-target activity at the CCR2 locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 5C and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Under experimental conditions that allow similar rates of on-target disruption using LP-directed ZFN delivery and plasmid-encoded ZFN production, off-target activity within the CCR2 locus is detected only after ZFN-encoding plasmid delivery.
source: By subsequent analyses of off-target disruption within the CCR2 locus of the same cells, we detected disruption (3%) induced by plasmid-encoded ZFNs, whereas indels and mismatches were not evident after ZFN protein transduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LP-directed protein transduction achieves locus targeting with an improved on-target/off-target cleavage ratio.
source: In summary, our findings lend strong support to the notion that locus targeting by LP-directed protein transduction is both effective and favored by an improved on-target/off-target cleavage ratio.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Efficient gene targeting can be achieved in a narrow window of ZFN exposure and activity outside this time window can cause toxicity without improving gene targeting efficiencies.
source: It is likely that efficient gene targeting can be achieved in a narrow window of ZFN exposure and that activity outside this time window can cause toxicity without improving gene targeting efficiencies (Porteus and Baltimore, 2003; Pruett-Miller et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Porteus and Baltimore, 2003; Pruett-Miller et al., 2009).

claim: The improvement in on-target/off-target cleavage ratio is a combined effect of efficient transduction and the short-term exposure to transduced ZFN proteins.
source: We reason that such improvement is a combined effect of efficient transduction and the short-term exposure to transduced ZFN proteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Lentiviral protein transduction of nuclease proteins represents a versatile alternative to current nuclease delivery techniques and will support continued efforts to promote safe genome editing therapies.
source: We anticipate that lentiviral protein transduction of nuclease proteins represents a versatile alternative to current nuclease delivery techniques and will support continued efforts to promote safe genome editing therapies.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future applications of the technology.

claim: Genomic engineers will likely strive to adapt LPs as carriers of Cas9 proteins for RNA-guided genome editing.
source: Likely, genomic engineers will strive to adapt LPs as carriers of Cas9 proteins for RNA-guided genome editing.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: IDLVs have been exploited to deliver ZFN-encoding genes.
source: Though IDLVs have been exploited to deliver ZFN-encoding genes (Lombardo et al., 2007), there are some clear inherent limitations to this approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Lombardo et al., 2007).

claim: Random integration of the vector can lead to insertional mutagenesis and sustained expression of ZFNs may cause cytotoxicity or chromosomal aberrations.
source: Firstly, random integration of the vector can lead to insertional mutagenesis and sustained expression of ZFNs may cause cytotoxicity or chromosomal aberrations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the risks of gene delivery methods.

claim: Two separate IDLVs are necessary to provide the two ZFNs and a third IDLV needs to be included if a donor template is required for homologous recombination.
source: Secondly, two separate IDLVs are necessary to provide the two ZFNs and a third IDLV needs to be included if a donor template is required for homologous recombination.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements of conventional IDLV-based ZFN delivery.

claim: Single IDLVs encoding both ZFNs have been described but do not perform as well as two separate IDLVs.
source: Single IDLVs encoding both ZFNs have recently been described, but these do not perform as well as two separate IDLVs (Joglekar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Joglekar et al., 2013).

claim: There are major difficulties in delivering TALENs by IDLVs due to an inherent propensity of lentiviral vectors to undergo recombination during reverse transcription.
source: Thirdly, due to the highly repetitive sequences in TALENs there are major difficulties in delivering these by IDLVs due to an inherent propensity of lentiviral vectors to undergo recombination during reverse transcription (Mikkelsen and Pedersen, 2000; Holkers et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Mikkelsen and Pedersen, 2000; Holkers et al., 2013).

claim: Lentiviral delivery of genes encoding re-coded TALE variants has been reported so far only for transcriptional activation.
source: In addition, lentiviral delivery of TALEN-encoding genes is further complicated by frequent recombination between the highly similar sequence repeats encoding the DNA-binding domain (Holkers et al., 2013), and lentiviral delivery of genes encoding re-coded TALE variants has been reported so far only for transcriptional activation (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Yang et al., 2013).

claim: Lentivirus-derived particles can be used as vehicles for different sets of designer nuclease proteins that are released from the Gag polypeptide upon virion maturation.
source: In this study, we have shown the feasibility of exploiting lentivirus-derived particles as vehicles for different sets of designer nuclease proteins that are released from the Gag polypeptide upon virion maturation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lentiviral protein delivery facilitates a short boost of protein activity that drives immediate targeted gene disruption (within 12 hr) in up to near one-fourth of the target alleles in a population of cells without the risks of permanently inserting copies of ZFN- or TALEN-encoding genes into the genome.
source: This approach facilitates a short boost of protein activity that drives immediate targeted gene disruption (within 12 hr) in up to near one-fourth of the target alleles in a population of cells without the risks of permanently inserting copies of ZFN- or TALEN-encoding genes into the genome.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: A lentiviral protein delivery approach benefits from effective lentiviral transduction and can easily be further customized by adapting different lentiviral pseudotypes to direct protein transduction to specific cell types of interest.
source: Moreover, as an alternative to protocols based on transfection of in vitro-transcribed RNA (Meng et al., 2008) or the cell-penetrating capability of purified ZFNs (Gaj et al., 2012), a lentiviral protein delivery approach benefits from effective lentiviral transduction and can easily be further customized by adapting different lentiviral pseudotypes to direct protein transduction to specific cell types of interest.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the approach, with citations to alternative methods (Meng et al., 2008; Gaj et al., 2012).

claim: At an MOI of approximately 34, 'all-in-one' vectors edited the reporter gene in up to 8% of treated cells.
source: At an MOI of approximately 34, such 'all-in-one' vectors edited the reporter gene in up to 8% of treated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The level of gene repair obtained with IDLVs carrying both ZFNs and the donor template is higher than previously reported repair rates obtained with the same pair of ZFNs under similar conditions using an analogous reporter system.
source: The level of gene repair obtained with IDLVs carrying both ZFNs and the donor template is higher than previously reported repair rates obtained with the same pair of ZFNs under similar conditions using an analogous reporter system (Urnov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature (Urnov et al., 2005) based on the data obtained in this study.

claim: A high rate of repair after protein transduction reflects the combined capacity of LPs to coordinately deliver pairs of nucleases by protein transduction and provide a donor for homologous recombination which is associated with the pre-integration complex and therefore is actively and efficiently translocated to the nucleus.
source: Although a direct comparison is not possible, we reason that a high rate of repair after protein transduction reflects the combined capacity of LPs to (i) coordinately deliver pairs of nucleases by protein transduction and (ii) provide a donor for homologous recombination which is associated with the pre-integration complex and therefore is actively and efficiently translocated to the nucleus (Coluccio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism, with citation to prior literature (Coluccio et al., 2013).

claim: The uptake of LP-delivered heterologous proteins is extremely limited relative to the very high levels of nuclear protein that can be achieved by standard plasmid DNA transfection.
source: We have previously observed that the uptake of LP-delivered heterologous proteins is extremely limited relative to the very high levels of nuclear protein that can be achieved by standard plasmid DNA transfection (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Cai et al., 2014).

claim: Editing is supported by the co-localization of ZFN proteins and the donor template within the pre-integration complex.
source: Based on these findings, we currently favor a model by which editing is further supported by the co-localization of ZFN proteins and the donor template within the pre-integration complex.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: TALENs have higher modularity than ZFNs and are becoming more routinely used due to the ease of production.
source: In comparison to ZFNs, TALENs have higher modularity and are becoming more routinely used due to the ease of production.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relative advantages of TALENs.

claim: TALENs are relatively large proteins (∼100 kDa), which may challenge their delivery.
source: However, TALENs are relatively large proteins (∼100 kDa), and this may challenge their delivery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the size of TALENs and an inference about delivery challenges.

claim: The majority of virally incorporated TALEN subunits are cleaved internally by the HIV-1 protease, which is suspected to limit the overall efficiency.
source: However, the majority of virally incorporated TALEN subunits are cleaved internally by the HIV-1 protease, which is suspected to limit the overall efficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: LPs loaded with CCR5-directed ZFNs cause disruptions in the CCR5 locus more effectively than ZFNs expressed from transfected plasmid DNA.
source: Interestingly, LPs loaded with CCR5-directed ZFNs caused disruptions in the CCR5 locus more effectively than ZFNs expressed from transfected plasmid DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In cells where LPs and plasmid-encoded ZFNs cause similar rates of CCR5 disruption, disruptions in the off-target CCR2 locus are evident with all concentrations of plasmid but detectable only with the highest and most effective dose of LPs.
source: In the same cells, disruptions in the off-target CCR2 locus were evident with all concentrations of plasmid but detectable only with the highest and most effective dose of LPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LP-delivered ZFNs target a safe harbor in the human genome with an improved on-target/off-target cleavage ratio.
source: These findings support the notion that LP-delivered ZFNs target a safe harbor in the human genome with an improved on-target/off-target cleavage ratio.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The IN D64V mutation renders the viral integrase incapable of catalyzing vector insertion.
source: We began by incorporating ZFNs targeting the egfp reporter gene (Urnov et al., 2005) into the gag gene of a packaging construct harboring the IN D64V mutation (Figure 1A), rendering the viral integrase (IN) incapable of catalyzing vector insertion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the D64V mutation in HIV-1 integrase.

claim: An HIV-1 protease cleavage site (SQNY/PIVQ) was included between the ZFN and the PH domain to allow the release of functional ZFN proteins during particle maturation.
source: An HIV-1 protease cleavage site (SQNY/PIVQ) was included between the ZFN and the PH domain to allow the release of functional ZFN proteins during particle maturation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Processing of ZFN-PH-GagPol polypeptides is not complete and proteolytic cleavage also occurs outside the inserted cleavage site.
source: Nevertheless, both longer and shorter forms of the ZFNs were evident (indicated by ZFN* in Figure 1B,C), suggesting that processing was not complete and that proteolytic cleavage had also occurred outside the inserted cleavage site, despite the fact that neither the ZFNs nor the PH domain contained naive HIV-1 cleavage sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on Western blot data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Neither the ZFNs nor the PH domain contain naive HIV-1 cleavage sites.
source: Nevertheless, both longer and shorter forms of the ZFNs were evident (indicated by ZFN* in Figure 1B,C), suggesting that processing was not complete and that proteolytic cleavage had also occurred outside the inserted cleavage site, despite the fact that neither the ZFNs nor the PH domain contained naive HIV-1 cleavage sites.
evidence: This is a statement about the design of the constructs.

claim: HEK293 cells and HKs contain the CCR5 Δ32 allele.
source: In HEK293 cells and HKs, we consistently observed an extra band (indicated by * in Figure 2, left panels) that was confirmed by sequencing to originate from the CCR5 Δ32 allele present in these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data confirming the identity of the extra band in Figure 2.

claim: The donor vector plasmid carries a 2.1-kb long sequence with homology to the egfp cassette present in the HEK293-eGFPmut cell line.
source: We generated, therefore, a donor vector plasmid carrying a 2.1-kb long sequence with homology to the egfp cassette present in the HEK293-eGFPmut cell line.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The donor vector does not itself express eGFP, but serves as donor for robust repair of egfp in HEK293-eGFPmut cells.
source: This vector did not itself express eGFP, but served as donor for robust repair of egfp (leading to eGFP production) in HEK293-eGFPmut cells that were transfected with donor-containing plasmid DNA and treated with increasing dosages of LP-ZFNLR(gfp) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reverse-transcribed vector serves as a recombination donor during HR-directed editing.
source: Next, the donor sequence was delivered by integrase-defective lentiviral vectors (IDLV/donor), allowing the reverse-transcribed vector to serve as a recombination donor during HR-directed editing.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and mechanism.

claim: Virions harboring Gag fused N-terminally to foreign proteins are strongly reduced in their capability of transferring vector RNA, but this capacity can be restored by including unfused GagPol in the virions.
source: Of note, we have consistently observed that virions harboring Gag fused N-terminally to foreign proteins are strongly reduced in their capability of transferring vector RNA (most likely due to complications during reverse transcription), but that this capacity can be restored by including unfused GagPol (encoded by pMDlg/pRRE-D64V) in the virions.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: The reduced capability of transferring vector RNA in virions with Gag fused N-terminally to foreign proteins is most likely due to complications during reverse transcription.
source: Of note, we have consistently observed that virions harboring Gag fused N-terminally to foreign proteins are strongly reduced in their capability of transferring vector RNA (most likely due to complications during reverse transcription), but that this capacity can be restored by including unfused GagPol (encoded by pMDlg/pRRE-D64V) in the virions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.
